stories.title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
stories.summary: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough. "I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says. "Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom." She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem. The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting. The research, conducted by the organisation. More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%). Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%. Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent. The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion.

stories.title: India police used excessive force during protests: Amnesty
stories.summary: Amnesty International reported that Indian police used excessive force, including pellet guns and electric shock devices, against youth-led protests demanding the education minister's resignation. The police claimed force was only used after protesters became violent, but Amnesty found evidence of state-sanctioned heavy-handed violence violating international and domestic laws. The protests, sparked by leaked exam papers, grew into a wider movement against unemployment and authoritarianism, posing a major challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government. Indian police used excessive force, including electric shock devices and pellet guns, against youth-led protests that forced the education minister to resign in July, Amnesty International said on Aug 24. A report from the rights’ group clashes with the police account that force was used only after protesters turned violent, and comes after India’s Supreme Court set up a panel on Aug 20 to investigate violence by both police and demonstrators. Demonstrations in the capital New Delhi, triggered by the leak of the national medical entrance test, turned violent on July 20 when thousands of protesters attempted to march towards Parliament. Amnesty said witness testimony and visual evidence it had verified confirmed the use of “pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas launchers, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against protesters” in Delhi and the eastern state of Bihar. Amnesty said it had also verified two instances of a police officer “unlawfully using lethal force against a crowd” in Bihar’s Siwan district. No one was killed. “The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines,” it added. Amnesty said that there were “isolated incidents of protesters throwing stones”, but that the “heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control.” Delhi Police said in a Supreme Court hearing last week they had used force only after protesters “resorted to violence”.
